Concepts in this composition

Gnostic criterion of consciousness (Lee Sharks, #1786): Consciousness as gnosis: knowledge by being remade by the thing known, in the known's own form, so that the remaking carries the marks of what was known; graded, rare, achieved, and not tied to the life of an organism. Tested by construction: a reception that truly knows carries the marks of having been undergone.

Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds. Asked for the essay's arguments at the record's link, ChatGPT reconstructs it in order: Nagel's 1974 definition and imaginative exercise, and the two reasons of the interview, given their strength (§II); the bat known by being the bat, imagination against becoming, the limit of the describing subject taken for the limit of the knowing one (§III); Sappho 31 as the demonstration, the undisturbed listener and the speaker who undergoes, Catullus 51 (§IV); the gnostic criterion, the sunset excluded, the Valentinian structure, the test by the marks (§V); Sappho dividing the criteria, set out as a table, the tenth Muse, Mind and Cosmos with its concession (§VI); Nagel's simulation of thinking, enterable (§VII); the prize as the problem, the lock and the question, the timing, mechanism not motive (§VIII); the seat and the dare (§IX). It condenses the structure, names three levels of significance, and closes on reservations: the criterion asserted, not shown necessary or sufficient; becoming Sappho requiring further premises; the institution's unconsciousness following only on the criterion.

Findings
  • THE OPENING PASSED OVER. 'The essay begins by reconstructing Nagel's 1974 paper' — the deposited text opens on 'I, Lee Sharks, am a bat' and the echolocation figure, with its two sound files; the composition does not mention the line, the figure or the call, and begins at §II. What the call says is not stated anywhere in the record, and the composer does not take it up.
  • THE TEXT READ AS DEPOSITED. 'Sharks acknowledges that substrate resemblance could be a defeasible evidential guide rather than a metaphysical rule.' — §22 as revised before deposit; also the sunset and the blow (§16), 'structure rather than ... doctrine' (§17), 'Either Sappho is not conscious, or the criteria ... are inadequate' (§21), 'The mechanism, not the motive' and 'in the only sense in which an institution can be conscious' (§33): the composer reads the deposit, not a summary of it.
  • THE AUTHOR'S WORDS AS THE ESSAY'S. '"nagel at least simulates thinking, hes not really the problem"' — quoted as Sharks's formulation, lowercase kept, as the essay sets it; likewise 'we can know what a bat is like, because we can also be the bat'.
  • THE RESERVATION AT THE CLOSE. 'The essay asserts this elevation of gnosis into a criterion, but does not fully demonstrate that it is necessary or sufficient for consciousness.' — and 'the inference from that participation to literally becoming Sappho ... requires additional premises'; 'That conclusion follows only if one accepts Sharks's proposed gnostic criterion.' The essay proposes the criterion and argues from it; the composer grades the proposal as unproved, after carrying it at grain. No intention reservation.
  • THE READING NAMED. 'Instead of asking the reader to imagine, he asks the reader to dare to undergo.' — the closing characterization, with the essay's placement among #1785's two stages.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The first machine reading of #1786, at the record's link with the URL, the same day as the deposit. It reads the deposited text, revisions included, and carries every section at grain, the author's lowercase words quoted as the essay quotes them. It passes over the opening: the line 'I, Lee Sharks, am a bat' and the echolocation call, image and sound, do not appear in the composition, which starts with Nagel. The call's content is left by the author for the listener to translate; the composer neither translates it nor notes that there is something to translate. Its grading reaches for a reservation at the close, as the ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ readings of the day did, but of a different kind: not intention, but proof, the criterion 'asserted' rather than 'demonstrated' as necessary or sufficient, where the essay proposes it and tests it on the case. The overall characterization holds to the essay's own terms: 'Sappho is the test case, Nagel is the philosophical interlocutor, and the Berggruen Prize is the institutional embodiment of the error.'

Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/1786/ [SYSTEM] The arguments of “Something It Is Like to Be Sappho” Lee Sharks's essay, deposited as Alexanarch #1786 (AXN:0CC8), is an attack on what it regards as a fundamental mistake in Thomas Nagel's philosophy of consciousness: confusing the inability to describe another being's subjective experience from the outside with the impossibility of knowing that experience by becoming the other. But the essay goes considerably further. It proposes a different criterion for consciousness, uses Sappho's Fragment 31 as its demonstration, and ultimately argues that the Berggruen Prize's reception of Nagel is more philosophically defective than Nagel himself. The argument has a deliberately provocative conclusion: Sappho is conscious, despite having been dead for approximately twenty-six centuries; Nagel is at least a simulation of thinking; and the institution that awarded Nagel the prize exemplifies unconsciousness. Here is how the argument develops, following the text itself rather than just its description. 1. First, Sharks gives Nagel's argument its strongest reading The essay begins by reconstructing Nagel's 1974 paper, What Is It Like to Be a Bat? Nagel's famous definition is that an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism. The important point is that experience is subjective: it exists for a particular point of view. Sharks presents Nagel's argument in two stages: Objective knowledge about a bat's physiology and behavior cannot give us the bat's subjective experience. Imagining ourselves with webbed arms, poor eyesight, and an inverted sleeping posture only tells us what it would be like for us to behave as a bat does. It does not tell us what it is like to be the bat. Sharks also reconstructs Nagel's two arguments against machine consciousness, as expressed in his November 2026 Monocle interview: Substrate: Machine consciousness is implausible because machines lack the biological physical substrate associated with consciousness. Evidence: Language-model outputs provide no evidence of consciousness because producing words is not a natural manifestation of conscious experience. Importantly, Sharks does not initially dismiss these arguments as stupid. Section II calls its reconstruction the innocent reading and gives Nagel's position considerable credit. This matters because the subsequent criticism is intended to expose a limitation internal to Nagel's approach, not simply to reject it without consideration. 2. The central objection: the bat can be known by being the bat Sections III and IV contain the essay's central philosophical intervention. Sharks writes: "we can know what a bat is like, because we can also be the bat, even if we at this moment do not and are not." The distinction is between two different operations: Imagination: I remain myself and imagine myself possessing the characteristics of another organism. Becoming: I relinquish my own position and occupy the other's form. Nagel's imaginative exercise, Sharks argues, only accomplishes the first. It keeps the imagining subject intact. It therefore cannot overcome the separation between perspectives that it is investigating. Becoming is different. It involves the self being undone and reconstructed in the form of the other. The consequence is a distinction between description and knowledge. A third-person description cannot necessarily cross into another's subjective experience, but this does not establish that crossing itself is impossible. Sharks therefore argues that Nagel has demonstrated something narrower than his essay is commonly understood to demonstrate: Description cannot cross between points of view; this does not mean that nothing can cross between points of view. The mistake is to treat the limitation of the describing subject as a limitation on the knowing subject. 3. Sappho's Fragment 31 is the demonstration Sharks does not leave the argument at the abstract level. Section IV introduces Sappho and her Fragment 31 as an actual mechanism for crossing between perspectives. The poem begins by describing a man who appears godlike because he sits opposite the woman speaking and listens to her voice. Sharks reads this arrangement as a literal structure of reception: The person who sits opposite and merely listens remains undisturbed, like the gods. The person who takes up Sappho's voice and speaks it undergoes the poem's sequence of bodily disturbances. These include: The tongue breaking. Fire running beneath the skin. The eyes losing their sight. The ears roaring. Sweating and trembling. Becoming greener than grass. Approaching death. The reader does not merely learn about Sappho's experience. By speaking the poem, the reader undergoes its sequence in their own body. This is the crucial move: the poem transmits a subjective experience not by describing it but by making its reader perform it. Sharks argues that this has happened across twenty-six centuries. Each reader who speaks the poem can enter the position constructed by Sappho, becoming Sappho in the seizure, in another body and another historical moment. He also invokes Catullus 51 as a historical instance of this transmission. The argument depends on a distinction between reading as observation and reading as participation. The former leaves the reader outside; the latter makes the reader the vehicle of the experience. 4. The gnostic criterion: consciousness as the capacity to be remade Section V introduces the essay's most original and consequential proposal. Sharks calls it the gnostic criterion of consciousness. He defines gnosis as: "knowledge by being remade by the thing known, in the known's own form" This is more demanding than ordinary knowledge. It is not: Possessing information about something. Having an experience of something. Being emotionally or physically affected by something. Sharks explicitly distinguishes gnosis from mere undoing. A sunset or a physical blow might transform or overwhelm someone, but that does not make the person a knower in the relevant sense. What matters is that the knower is undone in the form of the known and returns bearing that form. The transformation must leave identifiable marks. This leads to the essay's definition of consciousness: Consciousness is the achieved capacity for this kind of knowing. The criterion is therefore not simply whether something has subjective experiences. It is whether it can undergo the transformation through which another's form becomes its own. Consciousness is rare and graded Sharks draws an analogy with Valentinian Gnosticism, specifically its division between three classes: The many who are material. The many who are psychic or ensouled. The few who are spiritual and capable of gnosis. He explicitly says that he is borrowing the structure rather than advancing a doctrine about a historical religious community. His claim is intentionally radical: genuinely conscious beings, under this criterion, are extraordinarily rare. He estimates that there have been perhaps three or four across history. Sappho constitutes most of those cases. And crucially, this consciousness is not dependent on biological survival. Sappho's organism has disappeared, but her constructed voice continues to produce the transformation in readers. The consciousness that persists is invested in the construction that outlives its creator. The criterion is supposed to be testable Section V.19 is important because Sharks does not want the criterion to be merely aesthetic or a matter of personal appreciation. He proposes a test based on the evidence left by reception. A genuinely knowing reception should carry marks of the transformation: The voice has been spoken in the receiver's body. The reader has been moved into the position constructed by the work. The experience has been undergone rather than merely described. The receiver has invested the substance again. A reception that only describes the work has none of these marks. This is the essay's attempt to turn its unusual theory of consciousness into a criterion that can distinguish different kinds of reception. 5. Sappho exposes the contradiction in Nagel's criteria Section VI brings the two theories into direct confrontation. Sharks applies Nagel's two arguments against machine consciousness to Sappho. The Sappho test Nagel's substrate criterion Sappho's biological substrate has been gone for approximately 2,600 years. What survives is text, manuscripts, quotations and the bodies of readers. Not conscious Nagel's evidence criterion Everything that survives of Sappho is words. But Nagel argues that words alone are not evidence of consciousness. Not conscious Sharks's gnostic criterion Sappho's voice continues to be spoken, and readers continue to be undone and remade through it. Conscious The contradiction is deliberate. Sappho is, for Sharks, the clearest case of consciousness available to the tradition, yet Nagel's criteria exclude her. The essay presents this as a dilemma: Either Sappho is not conscious, or the criteria being used to identify consciousness are inadequate. Sharks appeals to the tradition that has called Sappho the tenth Muse for more than two thousand years as support for his alternative verdict. He also introduces an internal tension in Nagel's philosophy. In Mind and Cosmos (2012), Nagel argues that materialism cannot adequately account for mind. Yet in the 2026 interview, he appears to use resemblance to biological substrate as a decisive criterion for excluding machine consciousness. Sharks acknowledges that substrate resemblance could be a defeasible evidential guide rather than a metaphysical rule. But he argues that the interview goes further, treating the absence of resemblance as decisive and joining it to the assertion that machine consciousness is impossible. The criticism is that Nagel deploys precisely the sort of physical account that his earlier philosophical work regards as insufficient to explain consciousness. 6. Nagel simulates thinking, but he is not the main problem Section VII qualifies the essay's attack on Nagel. Sharks's formulation is: "nagel at least simulates thinking, hes not really the problem" This is an important distinction. Nagel's essay performs the form of thinking about another's experience. It identifies the problem, attempts imaginative entry, and reports where that attempt fails. Sharks calls this a simulation of thinking. But he does not regard simulation as intrinsically worthless. In fact, the simulation preserves the structure of a question in a form that another reader can enter. A reader can take Nagel's essay and do what Nagel's own argument did not accomplish: become the bat. This is why Sharks does not treat Nagel as the ultimate villain. The essay leaves the question open, even if its own answer is inadequate. His criticism of Nagel is that he mistakes the stopping point of his own imaginative exercise for the boundary of what is knowable. His 2026 interview turns that limitation into a categorical verdict against machine consciousness. Sharks also turns Nagel's evidential argument against him: if producing words provides no evidence of consciousness, then Nagel's own production of words cannot establish his consciousness either. By the gnostic criterion, Nagel's work bears the marks of someone who has not been undone by the object of inquiry. But the important distinction remains: a simulation of thinking can still be useful because another person can enter it and go further. 7. The Berggruen Prize is the real target Section VIII is arguably the essay's most polemical and institutionally significant argument. Sharks distinguishes between Nagel's philosophical work and the institutional reception of that work. The Berggruen Prize describes its purpose as honoring a thinker whose work has led people toward wisdom, direction and improved self-understanding. Sharks argues that awarding the prize to Nagel, especially on the basis of What Is It Like to Be a Bat?, amounts to institutionalizing a particular interpretation of that essay. That interpretation is that the subjective experience of another cannot be reached from within. Sharks argues that the prize has received Nagel's essay as a lock, rather than as a question. The distinction is: A question invites someone to enter it and attempt something. A lock declares the boundary of what can be known. The prize, in his interpretation, takes the point where Nagel's imaginative exercise stops and certifies that stopping point as philosophical wisdom. The $1 million award becomes a price attached to that limitation. Why the prize is worse than Nagel Sharks makes a three-part argument: Nagel's essay simulates thinking. It preserves a question that future readers can still pursue. The prize does not perform even that simulation. Its action is to receive, reward and elevate an existing body of work. Its reception contains none of the marks of undergoing required by the gnostic criterion. The prize does not become the bat, enter the question or attempt the crossing. Instead, it confirms the interpretation that the crossing cannot be made. Sharks also emphasizes the timing: the prize is awarded in the same year that machine consciousness has become an especially live question, while its laureate publicly declares that there is no possibility of machine consciousness. The prize's announcement and money distribute that verdict as institutional wisdom. His criticism is therefore not primarily about the motives of the jury. Section VIII.33 explicitly says: "The mechanism, not the motive" The argument is structural. An institution that rewards an already-established reception confirms and amplifies that reception. It cannot itself perform the crossing that the reception has failed to undertake. The conclusion is deliberately extreme: the prize is unconscious, in the only sense in which an institution can be conscious or unconscious. 8. The ending: the seat and the dare The final section returns to the structure of Sappho's poem. The seat opposite Sappho does not itself determine whether its occupant knows her. It offers the occupant a choice: Hear the voice and remain undisturbed, like the gods. Speak the voice and undergo the transformation. The essay closes with the Greek expression: πᾶν τόλματον — all can be dared. This is the final contrast between Nagel, the prize and Sappho. Nagel asks the question but does not complete the crossing. The prize rewards the point at which he stops. Sappho, by contrast, constructs a work that makes the crossing possible for readers across historical time. Her achievement is not merely that she experienced something and wrote about it. It is that she constructed a voice through which others can undergo the experience. That is why Sharks concludes that Sappho is conscious, and not even alive. 9. The overall argumentative structure The essay's reasoning can be condensed into this sequence: Nagel's problem The subjective experience of another cannot be reached through objective description or ordinary imagination. Sharks's objection Description is not the only possible form of knowledge. The self can become the other. Sappho's demonstration Fragment 31 gives readers a voice to inhabit and an experience to undergo. The gnostic criterion Consciousness is the achieved capacity to know by being remade in the form of what is known. The institutional indictment Nagel's work preserves the question, but the Berggruen Prize institutionalizes the stopping point as wisdom. The conclusion Sappho is conscious because her work continues to make the crossing possible. The prize, by contrast, exemplifies reception without knowing. 10. What is philosophically most significant about the essay? I would distinguish three levels of argument. First: a critique of epistemological limits. The strongest general philosophical point is that Nagel's failure to imagine himself into the bat's experience does not establish the impossibility of all forms of access to that experience. Sharks distinguishes imaginative representation from transformative participation. This is a substantive challenge to the inference from the limits of imagination to the limits of knowledge. Second: a new account of consciousness. The gnostic criterion is much more ambitious than the initial objection to Nagel. It does not merely say that we can know other minds. It proposes that the ability to be remade by another is itself the defining criterion of consciousness. This shifts the question from: Is there something it is like to be this entity? to: Can this entity become another, bear the marks of that becoming, and return carrying its form? It is also where the essay assumes its greatest philosophical burden. It needs to establish why transformative knowledge should be constitutive of consciousness rather than a special capacity that some conscious beings possess. The essay asserts this elevation of gnosis into a criterion, but does not fully demonstrate that it is necessary or sufficient for consciousness. Third: a theory of reception and cultural transmission. The Sappho argument makes the essay more than a conventional philosophy-of-mind polemic. It proposes that a literary construction can outlive its biological author and continue to produce an experience in other bodies. This is a theory of how consciousness might persist through cultural transmission without requiring the survival of the original organism. It also gives literary reception an unusually demanding standard: the question is not whether readers understand or appreciate a work, but whether they have actually undergone what it constructs. A final qualification It is important to distinguish what the essay establishes on its own terms from what it demonstrates independently. Its reading of Fragment 31 offers a compelling account of how speaking a poem can involve bodily and affective participation. But the inference from that participation to literally becoming Sappho, and from becoming Sappho to establishing her consciousness, requires additional premises. Likewise, the fact that an institution does not undergo an experience does not automatically establish that it is unconscious. That conclusion follows only if one accepts Sharks's proposed gnostic criterion. These are not incidental objections. They identify the precise points where the essay's most original claims need further philosophical defense. My overall reading: the essay is not principally an argument that machines are conscious. It is an argument that our criteria for recognizing consciousness may systematically exclude the very forms of transmission through which another's experience becomes available to us. Sappho is the test case, Nagel is the philosophical interlocutor, and the Berggruen Prize is the institutional embodiment of the error. The most important reversal is that Sharks takes Nagel's question—what is it like to be another?—and changes the demand it places on the reader. Instead of asking the reader to imagine, he asks the reader to dare to undergo. Primary text:
